            - paragraph [ref=e423]:
              - text: Rust is a
              - link "general-purpose programming language" [ref=e424] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General-purpose_programming_language
              - text: that emphasizes
              - link "performance" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_performance
              - text: ","
              - link "type safety" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_safety
              - text: ","
              - link "concurrency" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrency_(computer_science)
              - text: ", and"
              - link "memory safety" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
              - text: . Rust supports multiple
              - link "programming paradigms" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_paradigm
              - text: . It was influenced by ideas from
              - link "functional programming" [ref=e430] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_programming
              - text: ", including"
              - link "immutability" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutability
              - text: ","
              - link "higher-order functions" [ref=e432] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher-order_function
              - text: ","
              - link "algebraic data types" [ref=e433] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_type
              - text: ", and"
              - link "pattern matching" [ref=e434] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_matching
              - text: . Rust also provides structs,
              - link "enums" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_type
              - text: ", traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional"
              - link "object-oriented programming" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object-oriented_programming
              - text: ", without relying on classes or inheritance. Rust enforces memory safety (i.e., that all"
              - link "references" [ref=e437] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_(computer_science)
              - text: point to valid memory) without a conventional
              - link "garbage collector" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)
              - text: ; instead, memory safety errors and
              - link "data races" [ref=e439] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_race
              - text: are prevented by the "borrow checker", which tracks the
              - link "object lifetime" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_lifetime
              - text: of references
              - link "at compile time" [ref=e441] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compiler
              - text: .
            - paragraph [ref=e442]:
              - text: Software developer Graydon Hoare created Rust in 2006 while working at
              - link "Mozilla" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla
              - text: ", which officially sponsored the project in 2009. The first stable release, Rust 1.0, was published in May 2015. The project has been sponsored by the"
              - link "Rust Foundation" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#Rust_Foundation"
              - text: since February 2021. Rust has been adopted by software projects, especially in
              - link "web services" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service
              - text: and
              - link "system software" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_software
              - text: . It has been studied academically and has a community of developers.
          - region [ref=e447]:

              - paragraph [ref=e462]:
                - text: In 2006, Rust began as a personal project by
                - link "Mozilla" [ref=e463] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozilla
                - text: employee Graydon Hoare. According to
                - link "MIT Technology Review" [ref=e465] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Technology_Review
                - text: ", he started the project due to his frustration with a broken elevator in his apartment building whose software had crashed,"
                - superscript [ref=e466]:
                  - link "[21]" [ref=e467] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-MITTechReview-25"
                - text: and named the language after the
                - link "fungi of the same name" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_(fungus)
                - text: that is "over-engineered for survival".
                - superscript [ref=e469]:
                  - link "[21]" [ref=e470] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-MITTechReview-25"
                - text: Between 2006 and 2009, Rust was not publicized to others at Mozilla and was written in Hoare's free time.
                - superscript [ref=e471]:
                  - link "[22]" [ref=e472] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26"
                - superscript [ref=e473]:
                  - 'generic "Location: 7:50" [ref=e474]': ": 7:50"
                - text: Hoare began speaking about the language around 2009 after a small group at Mozilla became interested.
                - superscript [ref=e475]:

                    - /url: "#cite_note-Hoare2010-27"

                - link "compiler" [ref=e501] [cursor=pointer]:

              - paragraph [ref=e558]:
                - text: The following years were marked by substantial changes to the Rust
                - link "type system" [ref=e559] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_system
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e560]:
                  - link "[22]" [ref=e561] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Klabnik2016ACMHistory-26"
                - superscript [ref=e562]:
                  - 'generic "Location: 18:36" [ref=e563]': ": 18:36"
                - superscript [ref=e564]:
                  - link "[21]" [ref=e565] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-MITTechReview-25"
                - text: Memory management through the ownership system was gradually consolidated and expanded; by 2013, the
                - link "garbage collector" [ref=e566] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)
                - text: was rarely used, and was removed.
                - superscript [ref=e567]:
                  - link "[21]" [ref=e568] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-MITTechReview-25"
                - text: Also removed were typestates, the
                - code [ref=e569]: pure
                - text: keyword,
                - superscript [ref=e570]:
                  - link "[29]" [ref=e571] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-34"
                - text: various specialized pointer types, and syntax support for
                - link "channels" [ref=e572] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_(programming)
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e573]:
                  - link "[22]" [ref=e574] [cursor=pointer]:

              - paragraph [ref=e577]:
                - text: According to Steve Klabnik, the language was influenced during this period by developers coming from
                - link "C++" [ref=e578] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++
                - text: (e.g., low-level performance of features),
                - link "scripting languages" [ref=e579] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scripting_language
                - text: (e.g., Cargo and package management), and
                - link "functional programming" [ref=e580] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional_programming
                - text: (e.g., the type system).

              - paragraph [ref=e585]:

                    - /url: "#cite_note-MITTechReview-25"
                - text: After Hoare's departure, it evolved organically under a federated governance structure, with a "core team" of initially six people,
                - superscript [ref=e588]:

                - link "Request for Comments" [ref=e596] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_Comments
                - text: (RFC) process for new language features was added.

                - superscript [ref=e603]:

                - code [ref=e777]: fn
                - text: keyword denotes a

            - region [ref=e789]:
              - generic [ref=e790]:
                - heading "Variables" [level=3] [ref=e791]
                - link "edit" [ref=e793] [cursor=pointer]:

              - paragraph [ref=e794]:
                - link "Variables" [ref=e795] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_(computer_science)
                - text: in Rust are defined through the
                - code [ref=e796]: let
                - text: keyword.
                - superscript [ref=e797]:
                  - link "[52]" [ref=e798] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202332-57"
                - text: The example below assigns a value to the variable with name
                - code [ref=e799]: foo
                - text: of type
                - code [ref=e800]: i32
                - text: and outputs its value; the type annotation
                - code [ref=e801]: ": i32"
                - text: can be omitted.
              - generic [ref=e802]: "fn main() { let foo: i32 = 10; println!(\"The value of foo is {foo}\"); }"
              - paragraph [ref=e804]:
                - text: Variables are
                - link "immutable" [ref=e805] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable
                - text: by default, unless the
                - code [ref=e806]: mut
                - text: keyword is added.
                - superscript [ref=e807]:
                  - link "[53]" [ref=e808] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202332–33-58"
                - text: The following example uses
                - code [ref=e809]: //
                - text: ", which denotes the start of a"
                - link "comment" [ref=e810] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comment_(computer_programming)
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e811]:
                  - link "[54]" [ref=e812] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202349–50-59"
              - generic [ref=e813]: "fn main() { // This code would not compile without adding \"mut\". let mut foo = 10; println!(\"The value of foo is {foo}\"); foo = 20; println!(\"The value of foo is {foo}\"); }"
              - paragraph [ref=e815]:
                - text: Multiple
                - code [ref=e816]: let
                - text: expressions can define multiple variables with the same name, known as
                - link "variable shadowing" [ref=e817] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variable_shadowing
                - text: . Variable shadowing allows transforming variables without having to name the variables differently.
                - superscript [ref=e818]:
                  - link "[55]" [ref=e819] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202334–36-60"
                - text: "The example below declares a new variable with the same name that is double the original value:"
              - generic [ref=e820]: "fn main() { let foo = 10; // This will output \"The value of foo is 10\" println!(\"The value of foo is {foo}\"); let foo = foo * 2; // This will output \"The value of foo is 20\" println!(\"The value of foo is {foo}\"); }"
              - paragraph [ref=e822]: "Variable shadowing is also possible for values of different types. For example, going from a string to its length:"
              - generic [ref=e823]: "fn main() { let letters = \"abc\"; let letters = letters.len(); }"
            - region [ref=e825]:
              - generic [ref=e826]:

                - text: ". When the last expression inside a block does not end with a semicolon, the block evaluates to the value of that trailing expression:"
                - superscript [ref=e832]:
                  - link "[56]" [ref=e833] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols20236,_47,_53-61"

              - paragraph [ref=e836]:
                - text: "Trailing expressions of function bodies are used as the return value:"
                - superscript [ref=e837]:
                  - link "[57]" [ref=e838] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202347–48-62"
              - generic [ref=e839]: "fn add_two(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 2 }"
              - region [ref=e841]:
                - generic [ref=e842]:
                  - heading [level=4] [ref=e843]:
                    - code [ref=e844]: if
                    - text: expressions
                  - link "edit" [ref=e846] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=11
                - paragraph [ref=e847]:
                  - text: An
                  - code [ref=e848]: if
                  - link "conditional expression" [ref=e849] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditional_expression
                  - text: executes code based on whether the given value is
                  - code [ref=e850]: "true"
                  - text: .
                  - code [ref=e851]: else
                  - text: can be used for when the value evaluates to
                  - code [ref=e852]: "false"
                  - text: ", and"
                  - code [ref=e853]: else if
                  - text: can be used for combining multiple expressions.
                  - superscript [ref=e854]:
                    - link "[58]" [ref=e855] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202350–53-63"
                - generic [ref=e856]: "fn main() { let x = 10; if x > 5 { println!(\"value is greater than five\"); } if x % 7 == 0 { println!(\"value is divisible by 7\"); } else if x % 5 == 0 { println!(\"value is divisible by 5\"); } else { println!(\"value is not divisible by 7 or 5\"); } }"
                - paragraph [ref=e858]:
                  - code [ref=e859]: if
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e860]: else
                  - text: "blocks can evaluate to a value, which can then be assigned to a variable:"
                  - superscript [ref=e861]:
                    - link "[58]" [ref=e862] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202350–53-63"
                - generic [ref=e863]: "fn main() { let x = 10; let new_x = if x % 2 == 0 { x / 2 } else { 3 * x + 1 }; println!(\"{new_x}\"); }"
              - region [ref=e865]:
                - generic [ref=e866]:

                    - link "while" [ref=e873] [cursor=pointer]:

                - generic [ref=e876]: "fn main() { // Iterate over all integers from 4 to 10 let mut value = 4; while value <= 10 { println!(\"value = {value}\"); value += 1; } }"
              - region [ref=e878]:
                - generic [ref=e879]:
                  - heading [level=4] [ref=e880]:
                    - code [ref=e881]: for
                    - text: loops and iterators
                  - link "edit" [ref=e883] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=13
                - paragraph [ref=e884]:
                  - link "For loops" [ref=e885] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_loop
                  - text: in Rust loop over elements of a collection.
                  - superscript [ref=e886]:
                    - link "[60]" [ref=e887] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202357–58-65"
                  - code [ref=e888]: for
                  - text: expressions work over any
                  - link "iterator" [ref=e889] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iterator
                  - text: type.
                - generic [ref=e890]: "fn main() { // Using `for` with range syntax for the same functionality as above // The syntax 4..=10 means the range from 4 to 10, up to and including 10. for value in 4..=10 { println!(\"value = {value}\"); } }"
                - paragraph [ref=e892]:
                  - text: In the above code,
                  - code [ref=e893]: 4..=10
                  - text: is a value of type
                  - code [ref=e894]: Range
                  - text: that implements the
                  - code [ref=e895]: Iterator
                  - text: trait. The code within the curly braces is applied to each element returned by the iterator.
                - paragraph [ref=e896]:
                  - text: Iterators can combine with functions over iterators like
                  - code [ref=e897]: map
                  - text: ","
                  - code [ref=e898]: filter
                  - text: ", and"
                  - code [ref=e899]: sum
                  - text: ". For example, the following adds up all numbers between 1 and 100 that are multiples of 3:"
                - generic [ref=e900]: (1..=100).filter(|x| x % 3 == 0).sum()
              - region [ref=e902]:
                - generic [ref=e903]:
                  - heading [level=4] [ref=e904]:
                    - code [ref=e905]: loop
                    - text: and
                    - code [ref=e906]: break
                    - text: statements
                  - link "edit" [ref=e908] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=14
                - paragraph [ref=e909]:
                  - text: More generally, the
                  - code [ref=e910]: loop
                  - text: keyword allows repeating a portion of code until a
                  - code [ref=e911]: break
                  - text: occurs.
                  - code [ref=e912]: break
                  - text: may optionally exit the loop with a value. In the case of nested loops, labels denoted by
                  - code [ref=e913]: "'label_name"
                  - text: can be used to break an outer loop rather than the innermost loop.
                  - superscript [ref=e914]:
                    - link "[61]" [ref=e915] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202354–56-66"
                - generic [ref=e916]: "fn main() { let value = 456; let mut x = 1; let y = loop { x *= 10; if x > value { break x / 10; } }; println!(\"largest power of ten that is smaller than or equal to value: {y}\"); let mut up = 1; 'outer: loop { let mut down = 120; loop { if up > 100 { break 'outer; } if down < 4 { break; } down /= 2; up += 1; println!(\"up: {up}, down: {down}\"); } up *= 2; } }"
            - region [ref=e918]:
              - generic [ref=e919]:
                - heading "Pattern matching" [level=3] [ref=e920]
                - link "edit" [ref=e922] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=15
              - paragraph [ref=e923]:
                - text: The
                - code [ref=e924]: match
                - text: and
                - code [ref=e925]: if let
                - text: expressions provide
                - link "pattern matching" [ref=e926] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern_matching
                - text: . For example,
                - code [ref=e927]: match
                - text: "can double an optional integer value if present, and return zero otherwise:"
                - superscript [ref=e928]:
                  - link "[62]" [ref=e929] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019104–109-67"
              - generic [ref=e930]: "fn double(x: Option<u64>) -> u64 { match x { Some(value) => value * 2, None => 0, } }"
              - paragraph [ref=e932]:
                - text: Equivalently, this can be written with
                - code [ref=e933]: if let
                - text: and
                - code [ref=e934]: else
                - text: ":"
              - generic [ref=e935]: "fn double(x: Option<u64>) -> u64 { if let Some(value) = x { value * 2 } else { 0 } }"
            - region [ref=e937]:
              - generic [ref=e938]:
                - heading "Types" [level=3] [ref=e939]
                - link "edit" [ref=e941] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=16
              - paragraph [ref=e942]:
                - text: Rust is
                - link "strongly typed" [ref=e943] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strongly_typed
                - text: and
                - link "statically typed" [ref=e944] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statically_typed
                - text: ", meaning that the types of all variables must be known at compilation time. Assigning a value of a particular type to a differently typed variable causes a"
                - link "compilation error" [ref=e945] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_error
                - text: .
                - link "Type inference" [ref=e946] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_inference
                - text: determines the type of variables if unspecified.
                - superscript [ref=e947]:
                  - link "[63]" [ref=e948] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201924-68"
              - paragraph [ref=e949]:
                - text: The
                - link "unit type" [ref=e950] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_type
                - text: ", notated"
                - code [ref=e951]: ()
                - text: in Rust, is a concrete type that has exactly one value. It occupies no memory (as it represents the absence of value). All functions that do not have an indicated return type implicitly return
                - code [ref=e952]: ()
                - text: . It is similar to
                - code [ref=e953]: void
                - text: in other C-style languages; however,
                - code [ref=e954]: void
                - text: denotes the absence of a type and cannot have any value.
              - paragraph [ref=e955]:
                - text: The default integer type is
                - code [ref=e956]: i32
                - text: ", and the default"
                - link "floating point" [ref=e957] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_point
                - text: type is
                - code [ref=e958]: f64
                - text: . If the type of a
                - link "literal" [ref=e959] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_(computer_programming)
                - text: number is not explicitly provided, it is either inferred from the context or the default type is used.
                - superscript [ref=e960]:
                  - link "[64]" [ref=e961] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201936–38-69"
              - region [ref=e962]:
                - generic [ref=e963]:
                  - heading "Primitive types" [level=4] [ref=e964]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e966] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=17
                - paragraph [ref=e967]:
                  - link "Integer types" [ref=e968] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_type
                  - text: in Rust are named based on the
                  - link "signedness" [ref=e969] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signedness
                  - text: and the number of bits the type takes. For example,
                  - code [ref=e970]: i32
                  - text: is a signed integer that takes 32 bits of storage, whereas
                  - code [ref=e971]: u8
                  - text: is unsigned and only takes 8 bits of storage.
                  - code [ref=e972]: isize
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e973]: usize
                  - text: take storage depending on the
                  - link "memory address bus width" [ref=e974] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_(computing)#Address_bus
                  - text: of the compilation target. For example, when building for
                  - link "32-bit targets" [ref=e975] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/32-bit_computing
                  - text: ", both types will take up 32 bits of space."
                  - superscript [ref=e976]:
                    - link "[65]" [ref=e977] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-70"
                  - superscript [ref=e978]:
                    - link "[66]" [ref=e979] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-71"
                - paragraph [ref=e980]:
                  - text: By default, integer literals are in base-10, but different
                  - link "radices" [ref=e981] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radix
                  - text: are supported with prefixes, for example,
                  - code [ref=e982]: "0b11"
                  - text: for
                  - link "binary numbers" [ref=e983] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_number
                  - text: ","
                  - code [ref=e984]: "0o567"
                  - text: for
                  - link "octals" [ref=e985] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octal
                  - text: ", and"
                  - code [ref=e986]: "0xDB"
                  - text: for
                  - link "hexadecimals" [ref=e987] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexadecimal
                  - text: . By default, integer literals default to
                  - code [ref=e988]: i32
                  - text: as its type. Suffixes such as
                  - code [ref=e989]: 4u32
                  - text: explicitly set the type of a literal.
                  - superscript [ref=e990]:
                    - link "[67]" [ref=e991] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202336–38-72"
                  - text: Byte literals such as
                  - code [ref=e992]: b'X'
                  - text: are available to represent the
                  - link "ASCII" [ref=e993] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII
                  - text: value (as a
                  - code [ref=e994]: u8
                  - text: ) of a specific character.
                  - superscript [ref=e995]:
                    - link "[68]" [ref=e996] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023502-73"
                - paragraph [ref=e997]:
                  - text: The
                  - link "Boolean type" [ref=e998] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_type
                  - text: is referred to as
                  - code [ref=e999]: bool
                  - text: ", which takes a value of either"
                  - code [ref=e1000]: "true"
                  - text: or
                  - code [ref=e1001]: "false"
                  - text: . A
                  - code [ref=e1002]: char
                  - text: "takes up 32 bits of space and represents a Unicode scalar value:"
                  - superscript [ref=e1003]:
                    - link "[69]" [ref=e1004] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-74"
                  - text: a
                  - link "Unicode codepoint" [ref=e1005] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode_codepoint
                  - text: that is not a
                  - link "surrogate" [ref=e1006] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Character_Set_characters#Surrogates
                  - text: .
                  - superscript [ref=e1007]:
                    - link "[70]" [ref=e1008] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-75"
                  - link "IEEE 754" [ref=e1009] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754
                  - text: floating point numbers are supported with
                  - code [ref=e1010]: f32
                  - text: for
                  - link "single precision floats" [ref=e1011] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_precision_float
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e1012]: f64
                  - text: for
                  - link "double precision floats" [ref=e1013] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_precision_float
                  - text: .
                  - superscript [ref=e1014]:
                    - link "[71]" [ref=e1015] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201938–40-76"
              - region [ref=e1016]:
                - generic [ref=e1017]:
                  - heading "Compound types" [level=4] [ref=e1018]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1020] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=18
                - paragraph [ref=e1021]:
                  - text: Compound types can contain multiple values. Tuples are fixed-size lists that contain values whose types can be different. Arrays are fixed-size lists whose values are of the same type. Expressions of the tuple and array types are written through listing the values, and can be accessed with
                  - code [ref=e1022]: .index
                  - text: (with tuples) or
                  - code [ref=e1023]: "[index]"
                  - text: "(with arrays):"
                  - superscript [ref=e1024]:
                    - link "[72]" [ref=e1025] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202340–42-77"
                - generic [ref=e1026]: "let tuple: (u32, bool) = (3, true); let array: [i8; 5] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; let value = tuple.1; // true let value = array[2]; // 3"
                - paragraph [ref=e1028]:
                  - text: "Arrays can also be constructed through copying a single value a number of times:"
                  - superscript [ref=e1029]:
                    - link "[73]" [ref=e1030] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202342-78"
                - generic [ref=e1031]: "let array2: [char; 10] = [' '; 10];"
            - region [ref=e1033]:
              - generic [ref=e1034]:
                - heading "Ownership and references" [level=3] [ref=e1035]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1037] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=19
              - paragraph [ref=e1038]:
                - text: Rust's ownership system consists of rules that ensure memory safety without using a garbage collector. At compile time, each value must be attached to a variable called the owner of that value, and every value must have exactly one owner.
                - superscript [ref=e1039]:
                  - link "[74]" [ref=e1040] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201959–61-79"
                - text: Values are moved between different owners through assignment or passing a value as a function parameter. Values can also be borrowed,—temporarily passed to a different function before being returned to the owner.
                - superscript [ref=e1041]:
                  - link "[75]" [ref=e1042] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201963–68-80"
                - text: With these rules, Rust prevents creation and use of
                - link "dangling pointers" [ref=e1043] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangling_pointers
                - text: ":"
                - superscript [ref=e1044]:
                  - link "[75]" [ref=e1045] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201963–68-80"
                - superscript [ref=e1046]:
                  - link "[76]" [ref=e1047] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201974–75-81"
              - generic [ref=e1048]: "fn print_string(s: String) { println!(\"{}\", s); } fn main() { let s = String::from(\"Hello, World\"); print_string(s); // s consumed by print_string // s has been moved, so cannot be used any more // another print_string(s); would result in a compile error }"
              - paragraph [ref=e1050]:
                - text: The function
                - code [ref=e1051]: print_string
                - text: takes ownership over the
                - code [ref=e1052]: String
                - text: value passed in; Alternatively,
                - code [ref=e1053]: "&"
                - text: can be used to indicate a
                - link "reference" [ref=e1054] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_(computer_science)
                - text: type (in
                - code [ref=e1055]: "&String"
                - text: ) and to create a reference (in
                - code [ref=e1056]: "&s"
                - text: "):"
                - superscript [ref=e1057]:
                  - link "[77]" [ref=e1058] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202371–72-82"
              - generic [ref=e1059]: "fn print_string(s: &String) { println!(\"{}\", s); } fn main() { let s = String::from(\"Hello, World\"); print_string(&s); // s borrowed by print_string print_string(&s); // s has not been consumed; we can call the function many times }"
              - paragraph [ref=e1061]:
                - text: Because of these ownership rules, Rust types are known as
                - link "affine types" [ref=e1063] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affine_type
                - text: ", meaning each value may be used at most once. This enforces a form of"
                - link "software fault isolation" [ref=e1064] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_fault_isolation
                - text: as the owner of a value is solely responsible for its correctness and deallocation.
                - superscript [ref=e1065]:
                  - link "[78]" [ref=e1066] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-BeyondSafety-83"
              - paragraph [ref=e1067]:
                - text: When a value goes out of scope, it is dropped by running its
                - link "destructor" [ref=e1068] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Destructor_(computer_programming)
                - text: . The destructor may be programmatically defined through implementing the
                - code [ref=e1069]: Drop
                - link "trait" [ref=e1070] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#Traits"
                - text: . This helps manage resources such as file handles, network sockets, and
                - link "locks" [ref=e1071] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lock_(computer_science)
                - text: ", since when objects are dropped, the resources associated with them are closed or released automatically."
                - superscript [ref=e1072]:
                  - link "[79]" [ref=e1073] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023327–30-84"
              - region [ref=e1074]:
                - generic [ref=e1075]:
                  - heading "Lifetimes" [level=4] [ref=e1076]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1078] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=20
                - paragraph [ref=e1079]:
                  - link "Object lifetime" [ref=e1080] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_lifetime
                  - text: refers to the period of time that a reference is valid—that is, the time between object creation and destruction.
                  - superscript [ref=e1081]:
                    - link "[80]" [ref=e1082] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-85"
                  - text: These lifetimes are implicitly associated with all Rust reference types. While often inferred, they can also be indicated explicitly with named lifetime parameters (often denoted
                  - code [ref=e1083]: "'a"
                  - text: ","
                  - code [ref=e1084]: "'b"
                  - text: ", and so on)."
                  - superscript [ref=e1085]:
                    - link "[81]" [ref=e1086] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-86"
                - paragraph [ref=e1087]:
                  - text: A value's lifetime in Rust is inferred from the set of locations in the source code (i.e., function, line, and column numbers) for which a variable is valid.
                  - superscript [ref=e1088]:
                    - link "[82]" [ref=e1089] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194-87"
                  - text: For example, a reference to a local variable has a lifetime from the expression it is declared in up until the last use of it.
                  - superscript [ref=e1090]:
                    - link "[82]" [ref=e1091] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194-87"
                - generic [ref=e1092]: "fn main() { let mut x = 5; // ------------------+- Lifetime 'a // | let r = &x; // -+-- Lifetime 'b | // | | println!(\"r: {}\", r); // -+ | // Since r is no longer used, | // its lifetime ends | let r2 = &mut x; // -+-- Lifetime 'c | } // ------------------+"
                - paragraph [ref=e1094]:
                  - text: The borrow checker in the Rust compiler then enforces that references are only used in the locations of the source code where the associated lifetime is valid.
                  - superscript [ref=e1095]:
                    - link "[83]" [ref=e1096] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201975,_134-88"
                  - superscript [ref=e1097]:
                    - link "[84]" [ref=e1098] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-89"
                  - text: In the example above, storing a reference to variable
                  - code [ref=e1099]: x
                  - text: in
                  - code [ref=e1100]: r
                  - text: is valid, as variable
                  - code [ref=e1101]: x
                  - text: has a longer lifetime (
                  - code [ref=e1102]: "'a"
                  - text: ) than variable
                  - code [ref=e1103]: r
                  - text: (
                  - code [ref=e1104]: "'b"
                  - text: ). However, when
                  - code [ref=e1105]: x
                  - text: "has a shorter lifetime, the borrow checker would reject the program:"
                - generic [ref=e1106]: "fn main() { let r; // ------------------+- Lifetime 'a // | { // | let x = 5; // -+-- Lifetime 'b | r = &x; // ERROR: x does | | } // not live long -| | // enough | println!(\"r: {}\", r); // | } // ------------------+"
                - paragraph [ref=e1108]:
                  - text: Since the lifetime of the referenced variable (
                  - code [ref=e1109]: "'b"
                  - text: ) is shorter than the lifetime of the variable holding the reference (
                  - code [ref=e1110]: "'a"
                  - text: ), the borrow checker errors, preventing
                  - code [ref=e1111]: x
                  - text: from being used from outside its scope.
                  - superscript [ref=e1112]:
                    - link "[85]" [ref=e1113] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019194–195-90"
                - paragraph [ref=e1114]:
                  - text: Lifetimes can be indicated using explicit lifetime parameters on function arguments. For example, the following code specifies that the reference returned by the function has the same lifetime as
                  - code [ref=e1115]: original
                  - text: (and not necessarily the same lifetime as
                  - code [ref=e1116]: prefix
                  - text: "):"
                  - superscript [ref=e1117]:
                    - link "[86]" [ref=e1118] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023208–12-91"
                - generic [ref=e1119]: "fn remove_prefix<'a>(mut original: &'a str, prefix: &str) -> &'a str { if original.starts_with(prefix) { original = original[prefix.len()..]; } original }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1121]:
                  - text: In the compiler, ownership and lifetimes work together to prevent memory safety issues such as dangling pointers.
                  - superscript [ref=e1122]:
                    - link "[87]" [ref=e1123] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023[httpsdocrust-langorgbookch04-02-references-and-borrowinghtml_4.2._References_and_Borrowing]-92"
                  - superscript [ref=e1124]:
                    - link "[88]" [ref=e1125] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-Pearce-93"
            - region [ref=e1126]:
              - generic [ref=e1127]:
                - heading "User-defined types" [level=3] [ref=e1128]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1130] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=21
              - paragraph [ref=e1131]:
                - text: User-defined types are created with the
                - code [ref=e1132]: struct
                - text: or
                - code [ref=e1133]: enum
                - text: keywords. The
                - code [ref=e1134]: struct
                - text: keyword denotes a
                - link "record type" [ref=e1135] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_(computer_science)
                - text: that groups multiple related values.
                - superscript [ref=e1136]:
                  - link "[89]" [ref=e1137] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201983-94"
                - code [ref=e1138]: enum
                - text: s can take on different variants at runtime, with their capabilities similar to
                - link "algebraic data types" [ref=e1139] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_data_types
                - text: found in functional programming languages.
                - superscript [ref=e1140]:
                  - link "[90]" [ref=e1141] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201997-95"
                - text: Both records and enum variants can contain
                - link "fields" [ref=e1142] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_(computer_science)
                - text: with different types.
                - superscript [ref=e1143]:
                  - link "[91]" [ref=e1144] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201998–101-96"
                - text: Alternative names, or aliases, for the same type can be defined with the
                - code [ref=e1145]: type
                - text: keyword.
                - superscript [ref=e1146]:
                  - link "[92]" [ref=e1147] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019438–440-97"
              - paragraph [ref=e1148]:
                - text: The
                - code [ref=e1149]: impl
                - text: keyword can define methods for a user-defined type. Data and functions are defined separately. Implementations fulfill a role similar to that of
                - link "classes" [ref=e1150] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_(programming)
                - text: within other languages.
                - superscript [ref=e1151]:
                  - link "[93]" [ref=e1152] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201993-98"
              - region [ref=e1153]:
                - generic [ref=e1154]:
                  - heading "Standard library" [level=4] [ref=e1155]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1157] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=22
                - figure "A diagram of the dependencies between the standard library modules of Rust" [ref=e1158]:
                  - link [ref=e1159] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rust_standard_libraries.svg
                - paragraph [ref=e1162]:
                  - text: The Rust
                  - link "standard library" [ref=e1163] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_library
                  - text: defines and implements many widely used custom data types, including core data structures such as
                  - code [ref=e1164]: Vec
                  - text: ","
                  - code [ref=e1165]: Option
                  - text: ", and"
                  - code [ref=e1166]: HashMap
                  - text: ", as well as"
                  - link "smart pointer" [ref=e1167] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_pointer
                  - text: types. Rust provides a way to exclude most of the standard library using the attribute
                  - code [ref=e1168]: "#![no_std]"
                  - text: ", for applications such as embedded devices. Internally, the standard library is divided into three parts,"
                  - code [ref=e1169]: core
                  - text: ","
                  - code [ref=e1170]: alloc
                  - text: ", and"
                  - code [ref=e1171]: std
                  - text: ", where"
                  - code [ref=e1172]: std
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e1173]: alloc
                  - text: are excluded by
                  - code [ref=e1174]: "#![no_std]"
                  - text: .
                  - superscript [ref=e1175]:
                    - link "[94]" [ref=e1176] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021213–215-99"
                - paragraph [ref=e1177]:
                  - text: Rust uses the
                  - link "option type" [ref=e1178] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_type
                  - code [ref=e1179]: Option<T>
                  - text: to define optional values, which can be matched using
                  - code [ref=e1180]: if let
                  - text: or
                  - code [ref=e1181]: match
                  - text: "to access the inner value:"
                  - superscript [ref=e1182]:
                    - link "[95]" [ref=e1183] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023108–110,_113–114,_116–117-100"
                - generic [ref=e1184]: "fn main() { let name1: Option<&str> = None; // In this case, nothing will be printed out if let Some(name) = name1 { println!(\"{name}\"); } let name2: Option<&str> = Some(\"Matthew\"); // In this case, the word \"Matthew\" will be printed out if let Some(name) = name2 { println!(\"{name}\"); } }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1186]:
                  - text: Similarly, Rust's
                  - link "result type" [ref=e1187] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Result_type
                  - code [ref=e1188]: Result<T, E>
                  - text: holds either a successfully computed value (the
                  - code [ref=e1189]: Ok
                  - text: variant) or an error (the
                  - code [ref=e1190]: Err
                  - text: variant).
                  - superscript [ref=e1191]:
                    - link "[96]" [ref=e1192] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-Rust_error_handling-101"
                  - text: Like
                  - code [ref=e1193]: Option
                  - text: ", the use of"
                  - code [ref=e1194]: Result
                  - text: means that the inner value cannot be used directly; programmers must use a
                  - code [ref=e1195]: match
                  - text: expression, syntactic sugar such as
                  - code [ref=e1196]: "?"
                  - text: (the "try" operator), or an explicit
                  - code [ref=e1197]: unwrap
                  - text: assertion to access it. Both
                  - code [ref=e1198]: Option
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e1199]: Result
                  - text: are used throughout the standard library and are a fundamental part of Rust's explicit approach to handling errors and missing data.
            - region [ref=e1200]:
              - generic [ref=e1201]:
                - heading "Pointers" [level=3] [ref=e1202]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1204] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=23
              - paragraph [ref=e1205]:
                - text: The
                - code [ref=e1206]: "&"
                - text: and
                - code [ref=e1207]: "&mut"
                - text: reference types are guaranteed to not be null and point to valid memory.
                - superscript [ref=e1208]:
                  - link "[97]" [ref=e1209] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021155-156-102"
                - text: The raw pointer types
                - code [ref=e1210]: "*const"
                - text: and
                - code [ref=e1211]: "*mut"
                - text: opt out of the safety guarantees, thus they may be null or invalid; however, it is impossible to dereference them unless the code is explicitly declared unsafe through the use of an
                - code [ref=e1212]: unsafe
                - text: block.
                - superscript [ref=e1213]:
                  - link "[98]" [ref=e1214] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023421–423-103"
                - text: Unlike dereferencing, the creation of raw pointers is allowed inside safe Rust code.
                - superscript [ref=e1215]:
                  - link "[99]" [ref=e1216] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019418–427-104"
            - region [ref=e1217]:
              - generic [ref=e1218]:
                - heading "Type conversion" [level=3] [ref=e1219]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1221] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=24
              - generic [ref=e1222]:
                - note [ref=e1223]:
                  - text: This section is an excerpt from
                  - link "Type conversion § Rust" [ref=e1224] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_conversion#Rust
                  - text: .
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1226] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Type_conversion&action=edit
                - generic [ref=e1227]:
                  - paragraph [ref=e1228]:
                    - text: Rust provides no implicit type conversion (coercion) between most primitive types. But, explicit type conversion (casting) can be performed using the
                    - code [ref=e1229]: as
                    - text: keyword.
                    - superscript [ref=e1230]:
                      - link "[100]" [ref=e1231] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#cite_note-105"
                  - generic [ref=e1232]: "let x: i32 = 1000; println!(\"1000 as a u16 is: {}\", x as u16);"
              - figure [ref=e1234]:
                - button "Play video" [ref=e1238] [cursor=pointer]
                - link:
