            - region [ref=e1243]:
              - generic [ref=e1244]:
                - heading "Polymorphism" [level=3] [ref=e1245]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1247] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=25
              - paragraph [ref=e1248]:
                - text: Rust supports
                - link "polymorphism" [ref=e1249] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymorphism_(computer_science)
                - text: through
                - link "traits" [ref=e1250] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_(computer_programming)
                - text: ","
                - link "generic functions" [ref=e1251] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generic_function
                - text: ", and"
                - link "trait objects" [ref=e1252] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_object_(Rust)
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1253]:
                  - link "[101]" [ref=e1254] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023378-106"
              - region [ref=e1255]:
                - generic [ref=e1256]:
                  - heading "Traits" [level=4] [ref=e1257]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1259] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=26
                - paragraph [ref=e1260]:
                  - text: Common behavior between types is declared using traits and
                  - code [ref=e1261]: impl
                  - text: "blocks:"
                  - superscript [ref=e1262]:
                    - link "[102]" [ref=e1263] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107"
                - generic [ref=e1264]: "trait Zero: Sized { fn zero() -> Self; fn is_zero(&self) -> bool where Self: PartialEq, { self == &Zero::zero() } } impl Zero for u32 { fn zero() -> u32 { 0 } } impl Zero for f32 { fn zero() -> Self { 0.0 } }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1266]:
                  - text: The example above includes a method
                  - code [ref=e1267]: is_zero
                  - text: that provides a default implementation that may be overridden when implementing the trait.
                  - superscript [ref=e1268]:
                    - link "[102]" [ref=e1269] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107"
              - region [ref=e1270]:
                - generic [ref=e1271]:
                  - heading "Generic functions" [level=4] [ref=e1272]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1274] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=27
                - paragraph [ref=e1275]:
                  - text: A function can be made generic by adding type parameters inside angle brackets (
                  - code [ref=e1276]: <Num>
                  - text: "), which only allow types that implement the trait:"
                - generic [ref=e1277]: "// zero is a generic function with one type parameter, Num fn zero<Num: Zero>() -> Num { Num::zero() } fn main() { let a: u32 = zero(); let b: f32 = zero(); assert!(a.is_zero() && b.is_zero()); }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1279]:
                  - text: In the examples above,
                  - code [ref=e1280]: "Num: Zero"
                  - text: as well as
                  - code [ref=e1281]: "where Self: PartialEq"
                  - text: are trait bounds that constrain the type to only allow types that implement
                  - code [ref=e1282]: Zero
                  - text: or
                  - code [ref=e1283]: PartialEq
                  - text: .
                  - superscript [ref=e1284]:
                    - link "[102]" [ref=e1285] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023192–198-107"
                  - text: Within a trait or impl,
                  - code [ref=e1286]: Self
                  - text: refers to the type that the code is implementing.
                  - superscript [ref=e1287]:
                    - link "[103]" [ref=e1288] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols202398-108"
                - paragraph [ref=e1289]:
                  - text: Generics can be used in functions to allow implementing a behavior for different types without repeating the same code (see
                  - link "bounded parametric polymorphism" [ref=e1290] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_parametric_polymorphism
                  - text: ). Generic functions can be written in relation to other generics, without knowing the actual type.
                  - superscript [ref=e1291]:
                    - link "[104]" [ref=e1292] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019171–172,_205-109"
              - region [ref=e1293]:
                - generic [ref=e1294]:
                  - heading "Trait objects" [level=4] [ref=e1295]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1297] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=28
                - paragraph [ref=e1298]:
                  - text: By default, traits use
                  - link "static dispatch" [ref=e1299] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_dispatch
                  - text: ": the compiler"
                  - link "monomorphizes" [ref=e1300] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monomorphization
                  - text: the function for each concrete type instance, yielding performance equivalent to type-specific code at the cost of longer compile times and larger binaries.
                  - superscript [ref=e1301]:
                    - link "[105]" [ref=e1302] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023191–192-110"
                - paragraph [ref=e1303]:
                  - text: When the exact type is not known at compile time, Rust provides
                  - link "trait objects" [ref=e1304] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trait_object_(Rust)
                  - code [ref=e1305]: "&dyn Tr"
                  - text: and
                  - code [ref=e1306]: Box<dyn Tr>
                  - text: ", where"
                  - code [ref=e1307]: Tr
                  - text: is a trait.
                  - superscript [ref=e1308]:
                    - link "[106]" [ref=e1309] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019441–442-111"
                  - text: Trait object calls use
                  - link "dynamic dispatch" [ref=e1310] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_dispatch
                  - text: via a lookup table; a trait object is a "fat pointer" carrying both a data pointer and a method table pointer.
                  - superscript [ref=e1311]:
                    - link "[105]" [ref=e1312] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023191–192-110"
                  - text: This indirection adds a small runtime cost, but it keeps a single copy of the code and reduces binary size. Only "object-safe" traits are eligible to be used as trait objects.
                  - superscript [ref=e1313]:
                    - link "[107]" [ref=e1314] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset202125-112"
                - paragraph [ref=e1315]:
                  - text: This approach is similar to
                  - link "duck typing" [ref=e1316] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duck_typing
                  - text: ", where all data types that implement a given trait can be treated as functionally interchangeable."
                  - superscript [ref=e1317]:
                    - link "[108]" [ref=e1318] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023[httpsdocrust-langorgbookch18-02-trait-objectshtml_18.2._Using_Trait_Objects_That_Allow_for_Values_of_Different_Types]-113"
                  - text: The following example creates a list of objects where each object implements the
                  - code [ref=e1319]: Display
                  - text: "trait:"
                - generic [ref=e1320]: "use std::fmt::Display; let v: Vec<Box<dyn Display>> = vec![ Box::new(3), Box::new(5.0), Box::new(\"hi\"), ]; for x in v { println!(\"{x}\"); }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1322]:
                  - text: If an element in the list does not implement the
                  - code [ref=e1323]: Display
                  - text: trait, it will cause a compile-time error.
                  - superscript [ref=e1324]:
                    - link "[109]" [ref=e1325] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019379–380-114"
            - region [ref=e1326]:
              - generic [ref=e1327]:
                - heading "Memory management" [level=3] [ref=e1328]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1330] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=29
              - paragraph [ref=e1331]:
                - text: Rust does not use
                - link "garbage collection" [ref=e1332] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garbage_collection_(computer_science)
                - text: . Memory and other resources are instead managed through the "resource acquisition is initialization" convention,
                - superscript [ref=e1333]:
                  - link "[110]" [ref=e1334] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-115"
                - text: with optional
                - link "reference counting" [ref=e1335] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reference_counting
                - text: . Rust provides deterministic management of resources, with very low
                - link "overhead" [ref=e1336] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overhead_(computing)
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1337]:
                  - link "[111]" [ref=e1338] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-116"
                - text: Values are
                - link "allocated on the stack" [ref=e1339] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stack-based_memory_allocation
                - text: by default, and all
                - link "dynamic allocations" [ref=e1340] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_allocation
                - text: must be explicit.
                - superscript [ref=e1341]:
                  - link "[112]" [ref=e1342] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-117"
              - paragraph [ref=e1343]:
                - text: The built-in reference types using the
                - code [ref=e1344]: "&"
                - text: symbol do not involve run-time reference counting. The safety and validity of the underlying pointers are verified at compile time, preventing
                - link "dangling pointers" [ref=e1345] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangling_pointers
                - text: and other forms of
                - link "undefined behavior" [ref=e1346] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1347]:
                  - link "[113]" [ref=e1348] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols201970–75-118"
                - text: Rust's type system separates shared,
                - link "immutable" [ref=e1349] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immutable
                - text: references of the form
                - code [ref=e1350]: "&T"
                - text: from unique, mutable references of the form
                - code [ref=e1351]: "&mut T"
                - text: . A mutable reference can be coerced to an immutable reference, but not vice versa.
                - superscript [ref=e1352]:
                  - link "[114]" [ref=e1353] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019323-119"
            - region [ref=e1354]:
              - generic [ref=e1355]:
                - heading "Unsafe" [level=3] [ref=e1356]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1358] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=30
              - paragraph [ref=e1359]:
                - text: Rust's memory safety checks (See
                - link "#Safety" [ref=e1360] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#Safety"
                - text: ) may be circumvented through the use of
                - code [ref=e1361]: unsafe
                - text: blocks. This allows programmers to dereference arbitrary raw pointers, call external code, or perform other low-level functionality not allowed by safe Rust.
                - superscript [ref=e1362]:
                  - link "[115]" [ref=e1363] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023420–429-120"
                - text: Some low-level functionality enabled in this way includes
                - link "volatile memory access" [ref=e1364] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatile_(computer_programming)
                - text: ", architecture-specific intrinsics,"
                - link "type punning" [ref=e1365] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_punning
                - text: ", and inline assembly."
                - superscript [ref=e1366]:
                  - link "[116]" [ref=e1367] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNamara2021139,_376–379,_395-121"
              - paragraph [ref=e1368]:
                - text: Unsafe code is needed, for example, in the implementation of data structures.
                - superscript [ref=e1369]:
                  - link "[117]" [ref=e1370] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-UnsafeRustUse-122"
                - text: A frequently cited example is that it is difficult or impossible to implement
                - link "doubly linked lists" [ref=e1371] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubly_linked_list
                - text: in safe Rust.
                - superscript [ref=e1372]:
                  - link "[118]" [ref=e1373] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-123"
                - superscript [ref=e1374]:
                  - link "[119]" [ref=e1375] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-124"
                - superscript [ref=e1376]:
                  - link "[120]" [ref=e1377] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-125"
                - superscript [ref=e1378]:
                  - link "[121]" [ref=e1379] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-126"
              - paragraph [ref=e1380]:
                - text: Programmers using unsafe Rust are considered responsible for upholding Rust's memory and type safety requirements, for example, that no two mutable references exist pointing to the same location.
                - superscript [ref=e1381]:
                  - link "[122]" [ref=e1382] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-IsRustSafely-127"
                - text: If programmers write code that violates these requirements, this results in
                - link "undefined behavior" [ref=e1383] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undefined_behavior
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1384]:
                  - link "[122]" [ref=e1385] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-IsRustSafely-127"
                - text: The Rust documentation includes a list of behaviors considered undefined, including accessing dangling or misaligned pointers, or breaking the aliasing rules for references.
                - superscript [ref=e1386]:
                  - link "[123]" [ref=e1387] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-128"
            - region [ref=e1388]:
              - generic [ref=e1389]:
                - heading "Macros" [level=3] [ref=e1390]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1392] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=31
              - paragraph [ref=e1393]:
                - text: Macros allow the generation and transformation of Rust code to reduce repetition. Macros come in two forms, with declarative macros defined through
                - code [ref=e1394]: macro_rules!
                - text: ", and procedural macros, which are defined in separate crates."
                - superscript [ref=e1395]:
                  - link "[124]" [ref=e1396] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023449–455-129"
                - superscript [ref=e1397]:
                  - link "[125]" [ref=e1398] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021101–102-130"
              - region [ref=e1399]:
                - generic [ref=e1400]:
                  - heading "Declarative macros" [level=4] [ref=e1401]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1403] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=32
                - paragraph [ref=e1404]:
                  - text: A declarative macro (also called a "macro by example") is a macro, defined using the
                  - code [ref=e1405]: macro_rules!
                  - text: keyword, that uses pattern matching to determine its expansion.
                  - superscript [ref=e1406]:
                    - link "[126]" [ref=e1407] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-Rust_Ref._–_Macros_By_Example-131"
                  - superscript [ref=e1408]:
                    - link "[127]" [ref=e1409] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019446–448-132"
                  - text: "Below is an example that sums over all its arguments:"
                - generic [ref=e1410]: "macro_rules! sum { ( $initial:expr $(, $expr:expr )* $(,)? ) => { $initial $(+ $expr)* } } fn main() { let x = sum!(1, 2, 3); println!(\"{x}\"); // prints 6 }"
                - paragraph [ref=e1412]:
                  - text: In this example, the macro named
                  - code [ref=e1413]: sum
                  - text: is defined using the form
                  - code [ref=e1414]: "macro_rules! sum {"
                  - code [ref=e1415]: "(...) => { ... } }"
                  - text: . The first part inside the parentheses of the definition, the macro pattern
                  - code [ref=e1416]: ( $initial:expr $(, $expr:expr )* $(,)? )
                  - text: specifies the structure of input it can take. Here,
                  - code [ref=e1417]: $initial:expr
                  - text: represents the first expression, while
                  - code [ref=e1418]: $(, $expr:expr )*
                  - text: means there can be zero or more additional comma-separated expressions after it. The trailing
                  - code [ref=e1419]: $(,)?
                  - text: allows the caller to optionally include a final comma without causing an error. The second part, after the arrow
                  - code [ref=e1420]: =>
                  - text: ", describes what code will be generated when the macro is invoked. In this case,"
                  - code [ref=e1421]: $initial $(+ $expr)*
                  - text: means that the generated code will start with the first expression, followed by a
                  - code [ref=e1422]: +
                  - text: and each of the additional expressions in sequence. The
                  - code [ref=e1423]: "*"
                  - text: again means "repeat this pattern zero or more times". This means, when the macro is later called in line 8, as
                  - code [ref=e1424]: sum!(1, 2, 3)
                  - text: ", the macro will resolve to"
                  - code [ref=e1425]: 1 + 2 + 3
                  - text: representing the addition of all of the passed expressions.
              - region [ref=e1426]:
                - generic [ref=e1427]:
                  - heading "Procedural macros" [level=4] [ref=e1428]
                  - link "edit" [ref=e1430] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=33
                - paragraph [ref=e1431]:
                  - text: Procedural macros are Rust functions that run and modify the compiler's input
                  - link "token" [ref=e1432] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Token_(parser)
                  - text: stream, before any other components are compiled. They are generally more flexible than declarative macros, but are more difficult to maintain due to their complexity.
                  - superscript [ref=e1433]:
                    - link "[128]" [ref=e1434] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-rust-procedural-macros-133"
                  - superscript [ref=e1435]:
                    - link "[129]" [ref=e1436] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2019449–455-134"
                - paragraph [ref=e1437]: "Procedural macros come in three flavors:"
                - list [ref=e1438]:
                  - listitem [ref=e1439]:
                    - text: Function-like macros
                    - code [ref=e1440]: custom!(...)
                  - listitem [ref=e1441]:
                    - text: Derive macros
                    - code [ref=e1442]: "#[derive(CustomDerive)]"
                  - listitem [ref=e1443]:
                    - text: Attribute macros
                    - code [ref=e1444]: "#[custom_attribute]"
            - region [ref=e1445]:
              - generic [ref=e1446]:
                - heading "Interface with C and C++" [level=3] [ref=e1447]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1449] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=34
              - paragraph [ref=e1450]:
                - text: Rust supports the creation of
                - link "foreign function interfaces" [ref=e1451] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_function_interface
                - text: (FFI) through the
                - code [ref=e1452]: extern
                - text: keyword. A function that uses the C
                - link "calling convention" [ref=e1453] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calling_convention
                - text: can be written using
                - code [ref=e1454]: extern "C" fn
                - text: . Symbols can be exported from Rust to other languages through the
                - code [ref=e1455]: "#[unsafe(no_mangle)]"
                - text: attribute, and symbols can be imported into Rust through
                - code [ref=e1456]: extern
                - text: "blocks:"
                - superscript [ref=e1457]:
                  - link "[note 6]" [ref=e1458] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-136"
                - superscript [ref=e1459]:
                  - link "[131]" [ref=e1460] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021193–209-137"
              - generic [ref=e1461]: "#[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern \"C\" fn exported_from_rust(x: i32) -> i32 { x + 1 } unsafe extern \"C\" { fn imported_into_rust(x: i32) -> i32; }"
              - paragraph [ref=e1463]:
                - text: The
                - code [ref=e1464]: "#[repr(C)]"
                - text: attribute enables deterministic memory layouts for
                - code [ref=e1465]: struct
                - text: s and
                - code [ref=e1466]: enum
                - text: s for use across FFI boundaries.
                - superscript [ref=e1467]:
                  - link "[131]" [ref=e1468] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021193–209-137"
                - text: External libraries such as
                - code [ref=e1469]: bindgen
                - text: and
                - code [ref=e1470]: cxx
                - text: can generate Rust bindings for C/C++.
                - superscript [ref=e1471]:
                  - link "[131]" [ref=e1472] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset2021193–209-137"
                - superscript [ref=e1473]:
                  - link "[132]" [ref=e1474] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-138"
          - region [ref=e1475]:
            - generic [ref=e1476]:
              - heading "Safety" [level=2] [ref=e1477]
              - link "edit" [ref=e1479] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=35
            - paragraph [ref=e1480]:
              - link "Safety properties" [ref=e1481] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_properties
              - text: guaranteed by Rust include
              - link "memory safety" [ref=e1482] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_safety
              - text: ","
              - link "type safety" [ref=e1483] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_safety
              - text: ", and"
              - link "data race" [ref=e1484] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_race
              - text: freedom. As described above, these guarantees can be circumvented by using the
              - code [ref=e1485]: unsafe
              - text: keyword.
            - paragraph [ref=e1486]:
              - text: Memory safety includes the absence of dereferences to
              - link "null" [ref=e1487] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_pointer
              - text: ","
              - link "dangling" [ref=e1488] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangling_pointer
              - text: ", and misaligned"
              - link "pointers" [ref=e1489] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointer_(computer_programming)
              - text: ", and the absence of"
              - link "buffer overflows" [ref=e1490] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffer_overflow
              - text: and
              - link "double free" [ref=e1491] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_free
              - text: errors.
              - superscript [ref=e1492]:
                - link "[133]" [ref=e1493] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-cnet-139"
              - superscript [ref=e1494]:
                - link "[134]" [ref=e1495] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-lwn-140"
              - superscript [ref=e1496]:
                - link "[135]" [ref=e1497] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-The_Rustonomicon-141"
              - superscript [ref=e1498]:
                - link "[136]" [ref=e1499] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-Sensors-142"
            - paragraph [ref=e1500]:
              - link "Memory leaks" [ref=e1501] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_leak
              - text: are possible in safe Rust.
              - superscript [ref=e1502]:
                - link "[137]" [ref=e1503] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023343–346-143"
              - text: Memory leaks may occur as a result of creating reference-counted pointers that point at each other (a reference cycle)
              - superscript [ref=e1504]:
                - link "[137]" [ref=e1505] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKlabnikNichols2023343–346-143"
              - text: or can be deliberately created through calling
              - code [ref=e1506]: Box::leak
              - text: .
              - superscript [ref=e1507]:
                - link "[138]" [ref=e1508] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset20216-144"

              - link "standard library" [ref=e1522] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ", and other software development"
              - link "toolchain" [ref=e1523] [cursor=pointer]:

              - code [ref=e1524]: rustup

            - region [ref=e1528]:
              - generic [ref=e1529]:
                - heading "Compiler" [level=3] [ref=e1530]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1532] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=37
              - paragraph [ref=e1533]:
                - text: The
                - link "Rust compiler" [ref=e1534] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_compiler
                - text: ","
                - code [ref=e1535]: rustc
                - text: ", compiles Rust code into"
                - link "executables" [ref=e1536] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executable
                - text: . Source code is parsed as an
                - link "abstract syntax tree" [ref=e1537] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_syntax_tree
                - text: (AST) and lowered through multiple
                - link "intermediate representations" [ref=e1538] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_representation
                - text: (IRs). Next, a compiler backend is invoked to apply
                - link "optimizations" [ref=e1539] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimizing_compiler
                - text: and produce
                - link "object code" [ref=e1540] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_code
                - text: ", and a"
                - link "linker" [ref=e1541] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linker_(computing)
                - text: combines the object(s) into a single binary executable.
                - superscript [ref=e1542]:
                  - link "[140]" [ref=e1543] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-146"
              - paragraph [ref=e1544]:
                - text: The compiler uses
                - link "LLVM" [ref=e1545] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LLVM
                - text: as its default backend, and supports alternatives such as
                - link "GCC" [ref=e1546] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNU_Compiler_Collection
                - text: and
                - link "Cranelift" [ref=e1547] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranelift
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1548]:
                  - link "[141]" [ref=e1549] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-147"
                - text: The intention of those alternative backends is to increase platform coverage of Rust or to improve compilation times.
                - superscript [ref=e1550]:
                  - link "[142]" [ref=e1551] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-148"
                - superscript [ref=e1552]:
                  - link "[143]" [ref=e1553] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-149"
            - region [ref=e1554]:
              - generic [ref=e1555]:
                - heading "Cargo" [level=3] [ref=e1556]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1558] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=38
              - figure "Screenshot of crates.io in June 2022" [ref=e1559]:
                - link [ref=e1560] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crates.io_website.png
              - paragraph [ref=e1563]:
                - text: Cargo is Rust's
                - link "build system" [ref=e1564] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Build_system_(software_development)
                - text: and
                - link "package manager" [ref=e1565] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Package_manager
                - text: . It downloads, compiles, distributes, and uploads packages—called crates—that are maintained in an official registry. It also acts as a front-end for Clippy and other Rust components.
                - superscript [ref=e1566]:
                  - link "[144]" [ref=e1567] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Nature-150"
              - paragraph [ref=e1568]:
                - text: By default, Cargo sources its dependencies from the user-contributed registry crates.io.
                - link "Git" [ref=e1569] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Git
                - text: repositories, folders on the local filesystem, and other external sources can also be specified as dependencies.
                - superscript [ref=e1570]:
                  - link "[145]" [ref=e1571] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-151"
              - paragraph [ref=e1572]:
                - text: "Cargo supports reproducible builds through two metadata files: Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock."
                - superscript [ref=e1573]:
                  - link "[146]" [ref=e1574] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-152"
                - text: Cargo.toml declares each package used and its version requirements. Cargo.lock is generated automatically during dependency resolution and records exact versions of all dependencies, including
                - link "transitive dependencies" [ref=e1575] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transitive_dependency
                - text: .
                - superscript [ref=e1576]:
                  - link "[147]" [ref=e1577] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-153"

                - link "indentation" [ref=e1585] [cursor=pointer]:

                - text: to produce code in accordance with a common
                - link "programming style" [ref=e1586] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_style
                - text: . It can be invoked as a standalone program or through Cargo.

            - region [ref=e1604]:
              - generic [ref=e1605]:
                - heading "Versioning system" [level=3] [ref=e1606]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1608] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=41
              - paragraph [ref=e1609]:
                - text: Following Rust 1.0, new features are developed in nightly versions, released daily. During each six-week release cycle, changes to nightly versions are released to beta, while changes from the previous beta version are released to a new stable version.
                - superscript [ref=e1610]:
                  - link "[151]" [ref=e1611] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-Rust_Book_G-157"
              - paragraph [ref=e1612]:
                - text: Every two or three years, a new "edition" is produced. Editions are released to allow making limited
                - link "breaking changes" [ref=e1613] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking_changes
                - text: ", such as promoting"
                - code [ref=e1614]: await
                - text: to a keyword to support
                - link "async/await" [ref=e1615] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Async/await
                - text: features. Crates targeting different editions can interoperate with each other, so a crate can upgrade to a new edition even if its callers or its dependencies still target older editions. Migration to a new edition can be assisted with automated tooling.
                - superscript [ref=e1616]:
                  - link "[152]" [ref=e1617] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlandyOrendorffTindall2021176–177-158"
            - region [ref=e1618]:
              - generic [ref=e1619]:
                - heading "IDE support" [level=3] [ref=e1620]
                - link "edit" [ref=e1622] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=42
              - paragraph [ref=e1623]:
                - text: rust-analyzer is a set of
                - link "utilities" [ref=e1624] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_software
                - text: that provides
                - link "integrated development environments" [ref=e1625] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_development_environment
                - text: (IDEs) and
                - link "text editors" [ref=e1626] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_editor
                - text: with information about a Rust project through the
                - link "Language Server Protocol" [ref=e1627] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_Server_Protocol
                - text: . Among other features, this provides
                - link "autocomplete" [ref=e1628] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocomplete
                - text: and displays
                - link "compilation errors" [ref=e1629] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_error
                - text: during editing.
                - superscript [ref=e1630]:
                  - link "[153]" [ref=e1631] [cursor=pointer]:

          - region [ref=e1632]:
            - generic [ref=e1633]:
              - heading "Performance" [level=2] [ref=e1634]
              - link "edit" [ref=e1636] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Rust_(programming_language)&action=edit&section=43
            - paragraph [ref=e1637]:
              - text: Lacking garbage collection, Rust is often faster than other memory-safe languages.
              - superscript [ref=e1638]:
                - link "[154]" [ref=e1639] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-160"
              - superscript [ref=e1640]:
                - link "[78]" [ref=e1641] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-BeyondSafety-83"
              - superscript [ref=e1642]:
                - link "[155]" [ref=e1643] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-161"
              - text: Most of Rust's memory safety guarantees impose no runtime overhead,
              - superscript [ref=e1644]:
                - link "[156]" [ref=e1645] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNamara202111-162"
              - text: with the notable exception of
              - link "array indexing" [ref=e1646] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Array_(data_structure)
              - text: ", which is checked at runtime by default."
              - superscript [ref=e1647]:
                - link "[157]" [ref=e1648] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-SaferAtAnySpeed-163"
              - text: The performance impact of array indexing bounds checks varies, but can be significant in some cases.
              - superscript [ref=e1649]:
                - link "[157]" [ref=e1650] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-SaferAtAnySpeed-163"
            - paragraph [ref=e1651]:
              - text: Many of Rust's features are zero-cost abstractions, meaning they are optimized away at compile time and incur no runtime overhead.
              - superscript [ref=e1652]:
                - link "[158]" [ref=e1653] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNamara202119,_27-164"
              - text: The ownership and borrowing system permits
              - link "zero-copy" [ref=e1654] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-copy
              - text: implementations for some performance-sensitive tasks, such as
              - link "parsing" [ref=e1655] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing
              - text: .
              - superscript [ref=e1656]:
                - link "[159]" [ref=e1657] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-165"
              - link "Static dispatch" [ref=e1658] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Static_dispatch
              - text: is used by default to eliminate
              - link "method calls" [ref=e1659] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_call
              - text: ", except for methods called on dynamic trait objects."
              - superscript [ref=e1660]:
                - link "[160]" [ref=e1661] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcNamara202120-166"
              - text: The compiler uses
              - link "inline expansion" [ref=e1662] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inline_expansion
              - text: to eliminate
              - link "function calls" [ref=e1663] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_call
              - text: and statically dispatched method invocations.
              - superscript [ref=e1664]:
                - link "[161]" [ref=e1665] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-167"
            - paragraph [ref=e1666]:
              - text: Unlike in C and C++, the Rust compiler may reorder struct and enum elements unless a
              - code [ref=e1667]: "#[repr(C)]"
              - text: representation attribute is applied.
              - superscript [ref=e1668]:
                - link "[162]" [ref=e1669] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-168"
              - text: This can produce more efficient code in some cases.
              - superscript [ref=e1670]:
                - link "[163]" [ref=e1671] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGjengset202122-169"
            - paragraph [ref=e1672]:
              - text: Performance improvements in
              - link "LLVM" [ref=e1673] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LLVM
              - text: carry over to Rust using the default backend.
              - superscript [ref=e1674]:
                - link "[164]" [ref=e1675] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: "#cite_note-how-fast-is-rust-170"

            - paragraph [ref=e1731]:
              - text: In operating systems, the Linux kernel began introducing experimental support for Rust code in Version 6.1 in late 2022, as part of the
              - link "Rust for Linux" [ref=e1732] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_for_Linux
              - text: project.
